Many Outcomes

Session 10

2026-11-10

One question, many measurements

  • A study with many outcomes can answer two different questions:
    • Which outcomes moved? Test each outcome, and adjust for the number of tests.
    • Did the construct move? Combine the outcomes into one index, and test it once.
  • Every index assumes a measurement model: how the outcomes relate to the construct. The weights follow from the model.

Where many outcomes come from in AI evaluation

  • Several benchmarks or task families.
  • Rubric dimensions: accuracy, clarity, tone, safety.
  • Several judges, or human and judge scores of the same output.
  • Subgroups of users or items.
  • Prompt variants, seeds, and several models compared with one baseline.
  • Each of these is a family of tests.
  • Very rarely do you only have one thing you care about measuring in only one way.

How fast false positives accumulate

  • Lecture 06: \(K\) independent tests at 5% give at least one false positive with probability \(1 - 0.95^K\).
  • Correlated outcomes inflate it less, because their tests reject together.

A family is the set of tests behind one claim

  • A correction controls errors within a family: the tests that together support one claim.
    • “The assistant improves essays” rests on all eight rubric dimensions: one family.
    • “The assistant helps non-native speakers more” rests on the subgroup tests: a second family.
  • A single primary hypothesis is a family of one. It needs no correction.
  • Lecture 07’s PAP talked through how to deal with this for a single primary hypothesis.
  • Today: we expand beyond a single measure and think about multiple measures within a family and whether to combine them into an index.

Adjusting the tests

Two error rates

  • Of \(K\) hypotheses, the procedure rejects \(R\). Of those, \(V\) are true nulls.

\[\text{FWER} = \Pr(V \geq 1), \qquad \text{FDR} = \mathbb{E}\!\left[\frac{V}{\max(R, 1)}\right]\]

  • FWER protects every individual claim.
    • Even one false claim is costly: a safety finding, or the effect on a named outcome.
  • FDR protects the share of claims that are wrong.
    • To screen many candidates: which of 50 prompt variants to follow up.
  • \(\text{FDR} \leq \text{FWER}\), so FDR control rejects more.
    • FWER control is more conservative. It accepts fewer discoveries in exchange for fewer false ones.

Bonferroni and Holm

  • Bonferroni: reject \(H_k\) if \(p_k \leq \alpha / K\).
  • Holm: sort the p-values. Reject from the smallest up, until the first one above its threshold:

\[p_{(j)} > \frac{\alpha}{K - j + 1}\]

  • Both control FWER at \(\alpha\) under any dependence. Holm rejects at least as much.
  • Both are conservative with correlated outcomes.

Holm (1979), “A Simple Sequentially Rejective Multiple Test Procedure,” Scandinavian Journal of Statistics, 6(2).

Using the dependence: resampling step-down

  • Holm’s thresholds assume the worst case. The joint null distribution of the \(t\)-statistics gives exact ones.
  • Re-randomize \(Z\) (Westfall–Young) or bootstrap (Romano–Wolf), and step down:

\[\tilde p_{(j)} = \Pr\nolimits^*\Big(\max_{k \geq j} |t^*_{(k)}| \geq |t_{(j)}|\Big)\]

  • Correlated outcomes raise the thresholds, so it rejects more at the same FWER.
  • List, Shaikh & Xu (2019) extend it to subgroups and treatments.

Romano & Wolf (2005), Econometrica, 73(4). List, Shaikh & Xu (2019), Experimental Economics, 22(4).

Controlling the false discovery rate

  • Benjamini–Hochberg: reject \(H_{(1)}, \dots, H_{(j^*)}\), stepping up from the largest p-value:

\[j^* = \max\Big\{ j : p_{(j)} \leq \frac{j}{K}\,\alpha \Big\}\]

  • Valid under positive dependence, the usual case for one treatment’s outcomes.
  • Benjamini–Yekutieli: divide \(\alpha\) by \(\sum_j 1/j\) for any dependence.
  • Anderson (2008) reports sharpened q-values.

Benjamini & Hochberg (1995), JRSS-B, 57(1). Benjamini & Yekutieli (2001), Annals of Statistics, 29(4). Benjamini, Krieger & Yekutieli (2006), Biometrika, 93(3).

Simulation: power of each correction

  • 200 participants, 8 rubric dimensions. Three dimensions improve by 0.4 SD, five do not move.
  • Westfall–Young gains on Holm as the correlation rises. BH finds the most and keeps FDR under 5%, though its FWER exceeds 5% with weakly correlated outcomes. With eight outcomes, BY is stricter than Bonferroni.

Correcting the winner’s estimate

  • Lecture 07: the best of \(k\) estimates is inflated. The fix conditions on the selection.
  • The winner \(\hat k\) beat every rival, so \(X_{\hat k} \geq L\). With estimates correlated \(\rho\):

\[L = \max_{j \neq \hat k} \frac{X_j - \rho X_{\hat k}}{1 - \rho}\]

  • \(X_{\hat k}\) is normal truncated at \(L\). Solve \(F_\tau(X_{\hat k}) = \tfrac12\) for a median-unbiased estimate, and at \(\tfrac{\alpha}{2}\), \(1 - \tfrac{\alpha}{2}\) for the interval. With \(\bar\Phi = 1 - \Phi\):

\[F_\tau(X_{\hat k}) = 1 - \frac{\bar\Phi\big((X_{\hat k} - \tau)/\sigma\big)}{\bar\Phi\big((L - \tau)/\sigma\big)}\]

  • 10 variants, all truly +2. Naive: median +5.2, coverage 86%. Conditional: median +1.9, coverage 95%, 2.1× as wide. AKM’s hybrid interval narrows it.

Andrews, Kitagawa & McCloskey (2024), “Inference on Winners,” QJE, 139(1).

Building an index

An index changes the hypothesis

Separate targets

Measurements of one construct

  • An index is a weighted sum of standardized outcomes:

\[I_i = \sum_k w_k \tilde y_{ik}, \qquad \tilde y_{ik} = \frac{y_{ik} - \bar y^{(0)}_k}{s^{(0)}_k}\]

  • One test, no correction. Each index below is the right weighting for one measurement model (lecture 04).

Equal weights: the mean-effects index

  • Orient every outcome so higher is better, standardize by the control group, and average:

\[I_i = \frac{1}{K}\sum_{k=1}^{K} \tilde y_{ik}\]

  • Model: every outcome loads equally on \(\eta\). Errors are independent with equal variance (parallel measures).
  • Under that model, the average is the best linear estimate of \(\eta\).
  • Easy to explain and to register. Redundant outcomes count several times: four judge scores of one quality get four votes.

Kling, Liebman & Katz (2007), “Experimental Analysis of Neighborhood Effects,” Econometrica, 75(1).

Inverse-covariance weights: Anderson (2008)

  • Weight by the inverse covariance \(\hat\Sigma^{-1}\) of the standardized outcomes in the control group:

\[I_i = \frac{\mathbf{1}^\top \hat\Sigma^{-1} \tilde y_i}{\mathbf{1}^\top \hat\Sigma^{-1} \mathbf{1}}\]

  • Model: equal loadings on \(\eta\). Errors may be correlated: \(Y_3\) and \(Y_4\) are scored by the same LLM judge, and share its biases \(M\).
  • These are then the GLS weights: the minimum-variance linear estimate of \(\eta\).
  • An outcome that duplicates others gets less weight.

Anderson (2008), “Multiple Inference and Gender Differences in the Effects of Early Intervention,” JASA, 103(484).

Principal components

  • Weight by the first eigenvector of the correlation matrix \(\hat R\):

\[I_i = v_1^\top \tilde y_i, \qquad v_1 = \arg\max_{\|v\| = 1} v^\top \hat R\, v\]

  • Model: one factor, unequal loadings \(\lambda_k\), independent errors of equal variance. Then \(v_1 \propto \lambda\).
  • The weights follow shared variance. Biases shared by one judge model can dominate the first component.
  • Register the fitting sample, the sign, and the number of components.

A factor model, or IRT for binary items, estimates the loadings and error variances directly. Fu & Green (2026), arXiv:2505.21909.

Simulation: three indices, one study

  • Judge 1–4: one LLM judge scores four rubric dimensions, so they share its biases. Human 1–4: humans score the other four separately. The assistant raises essay quality \(\eta\) by 0.2.
Index Effect Power
Mean effects 0.30 55%
Anderson 0.33 61%
First PC 0.27 47%

Effect in control-group SDs of each index. 1000 simulated studies.

Weights from a target: the surrogate index

  • Goal: the effect on a long-run outcome \(Y\) (the final exam, 90-day retention) before \(Y\) is observed.
  • In an observational sample \(O\) with both \(S\) and \(Y\), fit \(\hat g(s) = \hat{\mathbb{E}}[Y \mid S = s, O]\).
  • In the experiment, use \(\hat g(S_i)\) as the outcome:

\[\hat\tau_Y = \frac{1}{n_1}\sum_{Z_i = 1} \hat g(S_i) - \frac{1}{n_0}\sum_{Z_i = 0} \hat g(S_i)\]

  • The weights come from predicting \(Y\). The target fixes them.

Athey, Chetty, Imbens & Kang (2019), “The Surrogate Index: Combining Short-Term Proxies to Estimate Long-Term Treatment Effects More Rapidly and Precisely,” NBER WP 26463.

What the surrogate index assumes

  • Surrogacy: \(Z \perp Y \mid S\). The whole effect on \(Y\) passes through \(S\). It fails with
    • a direct path \(Z \to Y\)
    • a shared cause \(U\) of \(S\) and \(Y\): conditioning on \(S\) opens \(Z \to S \leftarrow U \to Y\).
  • Comparability: \(Y \mid S\) has the same distribution in the observational sample and the experiment.
  • Failure: an assistant that writes the answers raises rubric scores \(S\) and lowers exam results \(Y\). The index predicts a gain.
  • Lecture 06’s surrogate labels use a simple proxy. The surrogate index combines many proxies to better represent the actual target.

Aggregating across benchmarks

Model Math Code Safety Writing Mean score Mean win rate
A 90 90 40 40 65.0 0.38
B 70 70 70 70 70.0 0.50
C 95 95 30 50 67.5 0.62
  • A leaderboard is an index over benchmarks. By mean score, B wins. By mean win rate (HELM), the share of head-to-head comparisons won averaged over benchmarks, C wins.
  • Rank-based rules are votes among benchmarks. Their rankings can change when a model is added or removed. More diverse benchmarks are less stable (Zhang & Hardt 2024).
  • Register the aggregation rule with the benchmark list.

Zhang & Hardt (2024), “Inherent Trade-Offs between Diversity and Stability in Multi-Task Benchmarks,” ICML. Liang et al. (2022), HELM.

Testing all outcomes jointly

Is anything moving? Omnibus tests

  • An index tests one weighted sum, and its weights define the construct. A joint test of all \(K\) effects needs no weights. It asks whether any outcome moved: \(\tau_1 = \dots = \tau_K = 0\).
  • The Wald statistic uses the full covariance of the \(K\) estimated effects:

\[W = \hat\tau^\top \hat V^{-1} \hat\tau, \qquad \hat V = \frac{S_1}{n_1} + \frac{S_0}{n_0}\]

  • \(S_z\) is the covariance matrix of the outcomes in arm \(z\). Under the null, \(W \approx \chi^2_K\).
  • Randomization inference: under the sharp null, \(Y_{ik}(1) = Y_{ik}(0)\) for every unit and outcome. Re-randomize \(Z\), recompute \(W\), and report the share of draws with \(W^* \geq W\). This is exact in finite samples.

Young (2019), “Channeling Fisher,” QJE. Caughey, Dafoe & Seawright (2017), “Nonparametric Combination (NPC),” Political Analysis.

Simulation: which test finds the effect

  • 200 participants, half get a writing assistant. Essays are scored on 8 rubric dimensions, correlated \(\rho = 0.3\). Effects are in control-SD units.
  • The index wins when the effects share a sign. The omnibus test wins otherwise, because it uses the correlation between dimensions. Holm answers a narrower question: which dimension moved.

Inverse regression

  • Regress the treatment on all outcomes at once:

\[Z_i = \alpha + \beta^\top \tilde y_i + e_i\]

  • Testing \(\beta = 0\) asks whether the outcome vector differs between arms. For OLS this \(F\) test is Hotelling’s \(T^2\), an omnibus test.
  • Each \(\beta_k\) shows how outcome \(k\) separates the arms, holding the other outcomes fixed.
  • Zhang, Li & Ding (2025) develop this approach for causal inference with multiple outcomes.

Zhang, Li & Ding (2025), “Inverse Regression for Causal Inference with Multiple Outcomes,” arXiv:2509.12587.

Other responses

Partial pooling

  • Model the \(K\) effects as draws from one distribution:

\[\hat\tau_k \sim N(\tau_k, s_k^2), \qquad \tau_k \sim N(\mu, \sigma^2)\]

  • Each estimate moves toward the common mean, the noisy ones most:

\[\tilde\tau_k = (1 - B_k)\,\hat\tau_k + B_k\,\hat\mu, \qquad B_k = \frac{s_k^2}{s_k^2 + \hat\sigma^2}\]

  • The extreme estimates that drive false positives shrink most. The intervals come from the model, with no further correction.
  • Assumption: the \(K\) effects are exchangeable. This fits rubric dimensions, subgroups, or prompt variants on a common scale.

Gelman, Hill & Yajima (2012), “Why We (Usually) Don’t Have to Worry About Multiple Comparisons,” JREE, 5(2).

Matching the response to the question

  • This named outcome moved: FWER control. Holm or Westfall–Young.
  • Most of these discoveries are real: FDR control. Benjamini–Hochberg.
  • The construct moved: an index, weighted by the measurement model you believe.
  • The long-run outcome moved: a surrogate index, if surrogacy is credible.
  • Something moved: an omnibus test.
  • The best arm is this much better: fresh items, or winner’s-curse intervals.
  • The method follows from the claim you want to make.

Heterogeneous effects

Subgroups: which null?

  • With \(G\) subgroups, there are \(G\) effects \(\tau_1, \dots, \tau_G\). Two different nulls:
    • No effect anywhere: \(\tau_1 = \dots = \tau_G = 0\). A joint test, like the omnibus test.
    • No heterogeneity: \(\tau_1 = \dots = \tau_G\). The effect may be large, but it is the same in every group.
  • A significant effect in one group and not another is no evidence of heterogeneity. Test the difference:

\[\widehat{\mathrm{SE}}(\hat\tau_A - \hat\tau_B) = \sqrt{\widehat{\mathrm{SE}}(\hat\tau_A)^2 + \widehat{\mathrm{SE}}(\hat\tau_B)^2}\]

  • Registered subgroups get a correction within their family. Unregistered subgroups are exploratory.

Continuous moderators

  • Lecture 06’s Lin estimator already interacts \(Z\) with \(X\). The interaction is the heterogeneity estimate:

\[Y_i = \alpha + \tau Z_i + \gamma X_i + \delta Z_i X_i + \varepsilon_i, \qquad \tau(x) = \tau + \delta x\]

  • \(\delta = 0\) is the no-heterogeneity null for \(X\).
  • The model assumes the effect changes linearly in \(x\), and that both arms have data across the range of \(x\).
  • Check both: estimate the effect within bins of \(X\) (e.g., terciles) and compare with the line.

Hainmueller, Mummolo & Xu (2019), “How Much Should We Trust Estimates from Multiplicative Interaction Models?,” Political Analysis, 27(2).

The oracle regression

  • If we saw each unit’s effect \(\tau_i = Y_i(1) - Y_i(0)\), heterogeneity would be an ordinary regression:

\[\hat\beta = \arg\min_\beta \sum_i \big(\tau_i - X_i^\top \beta\big)^2\]

  • Each unit reveals \(Y_i(1)\) or \(Y_i(0)\), never both. \(\tau_i\) is never observed.
  • We need an observable quantity whose regression on \(X\) has the same target, \(\tau(x) = \mathbb{E}[\tau_i \mid X_i = x]\).

Robinson’s decomposition and the R-learner

  • Frisch–Waugh–Lovell: the coefficient on \(Z\) in \(Y \sim Z + X\) is the regression of residualized \(Y\) on residualized \(Z\).
  • Robinson (1988) extends this to effects that vary with \(X\). With \(m(x) = \mathbb{E}[Y \mid X = x]\) and \(e(x) = \Pr(Z = 1 \mid X = x)\):

\[Y_i - m(X_i) = \big(Z_i - e(X_i)\big)\,\tau(X_i) + \varepsilon_i\]

  • In an experiment \(e = \tfrac12\) is known. Fit \(\hat m\) on held-out folds. Then regress, with weights \((Z_i - e)^2\):

\[\tilde\tau_i = \frac{Y_i - \hat m(X_i)}{Z_i - e} \quad \text{on } X_i\]

  • This is the oracle regression, with the observable \(\tilde\tau_i\) in place of \(\tau_i\): \(\mathbb{E}[\tilde\tau_i \mid X_i] = \tau(X_i)\).

Robinson (1988), Econometrica, 56(4). Nie & Wager (2021), “Quasi-Oracle Estimation of Heterogeneous Treatment Effects,” Biometrika, 108(2).

Simulation: oracle and R-learner

  • 400 participants. The assistant helps weaker writers more: \(\tau(x) = 0.4 - 0.25x\), with \(x\) the prior writing score in SDs.
  • Both regressions target \(\tau(x)\). The pseudo-outcome is far noisier than \(\tau_i\) (many points fall outside this window), so the R-learner needs more data for the same precision.
